body:
Lothal: a town associated with a tidal dock

Lothal is one of the most important Harappan sites in Gujarat for understanding trade and craft production. It was situated near the Bhogava River, a tributary of the Sabarmati, with access towards the Gulf of Khambhat, also called the Gulf of Cambay.

Lothal developed as a centre where goods could be manufactured, stored and exchanged. Its major trade-related features include a bead-making workshop, a structure identified as a warehouse and a large basin commonly interpreted as a dockyard.

The large basin

A substantial brick-lined basin lies beside the settlement. It measures approximately 217 metres in length according to the UNESCO World Heritage Centre's Lothal Tentative List description. The structure has commonly been identified as a tidal dockyard, with arrangements that could have allowed boats to enter or leave through an ancient water channel.

The dockyard interpretation is widely used in textbook accounts and is supported by the surrounding maritime evidence. However, the exact purpose of the basin has been questioned by some researchers, so it is more precise to describe it as a structure commonly identified as a dockyard rather than treating every aspect of its use as conclusively established.

Warehouse and sealings

Another important structure at Lothal has been identified as a warehouse. Seals and clay sealings were found in association with this area.

These finds are consistent with the handling of packaged goods. A sealing could identify a consignment and help indicate whether it remained unopened during movement or storage.

Bead-making centre

Lothal was also a centre for manufacturing beads from semi-precious stones, particularly carnelian. Its location near sources of raw materials and access to transport networks made it well suited to specialised production and exchange.

Dholavira: an important trading and manufacturing centre

Dholavira is situated on Khadir Bet in the Rann of Kutch, Gujarat. It was a major Harappan urban settlement with extensive planning, water-management structures and evidence of craft activity.

Objects made from copper, shell, stone, ivory and valuable materials have been recovered at Dholavira. Evidence of bead-processing activities and contacts with other Harappan settlements demonstrates its economic importance.

The UNESCO World Heritage Centre also identifies evidence of Dholavira's interregional contacts with areas including Mesopotamia and the Oman peninsula.

Dholavira's strategic location helped connect Gujarat's resources and settlements with wider exchange networks. However, Dholavira should not be confused with Lothal's dockyard. Dholavira is especially important as a major urban, manufacturing and trading centre, whereas Lothal is particularly associated with a large basin interpreted as a tidal dock.

Nageshwar: a coastal shell-working centre

Nageshwar was a Harappan settlement in coastal Gujarat associated with the production of shell objects.

Marine shells were worked into articles such as bangles, ladles and decorative inlays. These finished products could then be transported to settlements farther inland.

Nageshwar illustrates an important distinction: a coastal site may be economically significant because it supplies marine materials, even without evidence that it possessed a large dockyard.

Distinguish the 3 Gujarat sites

  • Lothal: bead-making, storage and a large basin commonly interpreted as a dockyard.
  • Dholavira: major Harappan urban centre on Khadir Bet, with manufacturing and interregional trade connections.
  • Nageshwar: coastal settlement associated with shell-working.

Prelims focus

  • Lothal is associated with the Bhogava River and the Gulf of Khambhat.
  • Lothal is known for a large basin commonly identified as a tidal dockyard.
  • Seals and sealings were discovered in association with the warehouse area at Lothal.
  • Dholavira is situated on Khadir Bet in Kutch.
  • Nageshwar is associated with shell-working.
  • Trap: The famous dockyard association belongs to Lothal, not Dholavira.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 4, 'In the Earliest Cities', pp. 39–40; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones', pp. 11–13; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Archaeological remains of a Harappa Port-Town, Lothal', Tentative List 5918, Description, consulted 17 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Dholavira: a Harappan City', World Heritage List 1645, Brief Synthesis and Outstanding Universal Value, consulted 17 November 2026.]
title: Gujarat's Key Harappan Trade Sites

body:
The sea linked the Indus region with the Persian Gulf

Harappan maritime trade connected settlements of the Indian subcontinent with communities around the Arabian Sea and Persian Gulf. Archaeological finds and Mesopotamian references show that goods moved across this wider region during the third millennium BCE.

The coast of Gujarat and Sindh provided access to the Arabian Sea. From this region, maritime connections extended westward towards the Makran coast, the Oman peninsula, Bahrain and southern Mesopotamia.

These places formed parts of a wider network. The evidence does not establish one compulsory route followed by every vessel. Goods might travel through intermediate settlements, and different journeys could involve different coastal stops.

Harappan coastal connections

Gujarat and Sindh: Their coastal settlements gave access to the Arabian Sea. Lothal, near the Gulf of Khambhat, is particularly associated with maritime exchange.

Makran coast: Harappan outposts such as Sutkagen-dor and Sotka Koh were located along this western coastal region. Their locations support the possibility of contacts between the Indus region and areas farther west, although their precise roles in overseas shipping are not fully established.

Oman: The Oman peninsula was connected with the movement of copper and other commodities. Harappan-type jars found at Omani sites provide evidence of contact.

Bahrain and Mesopotamia: Objects and written references indicate connections with trading communities around the Persian Gulf and the cities of southern Mesopotamia.

Evidence for maritime exchange

Several kinds of evidence support the existence of Harappan maritime contacts.

  • Representations of boats: Harappan seals and other objects depict watercraft, indicating familiarity with boats and their use.
  • Coastal settlements: Harappan sites along the Gujarat, Sindh and Makran coasts demonstrate the civilisation's presence near maritime routes.
  • Lothal: Its large basin, commonly identified as a dockyard, together with storage-related structures, anchors and other finds, supports its association with waterborne exchange.
  • Finds in Oman: Large Harappan-type jars have been discovered at Omani sites, demonstrating material contact between the regions.
  • Objects in the Persian Gulf: Harappan-style seals, weights and ornaments found outside the Indus region support long-distance connections.

Why intermediate trading centres mattered

Goods did not necessarily travel directly from their original source to their final destination. A trader could acquire goods from one settlement and exchange them at another, where they might be carried farther by someone else.

This helps explain why a commodity from the Indian subcontinent could appear in Mesopotamia without proving that the original producer personally travelled there.

It also explains why the presence of Harappan objects in a foreign region demonstrates contact but does not automatically establish the identity of the ship's crew or the complete route followed.

Maritime contact between the Harappan region and West Asia is supported by several independent kinds of evidence. The exact voyages, shipping schedules and routes of individual consignments remain uncertain.

Prelims focus

  • Harappan maritime connections extended through the Arabian Sea and Persian Gulf.
  • Important connected regions included Gujarat, Sindh, Oman, Bahrain and Mesopotamia.
  • Sutkagen-dor and Sotka Koh were Harappan settlements on the Makran coast.
  • Harappan-type jars have been found in Oman.
  • Boat depictions and coastal archaeological finds support the existence of waterborne exchange.
  • Trap: The presence of an imported object does not prove that it travelled directly from its place of origin without intermediate trading centres.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones', Sections 6.1 and 6.2, pp. 12–15, and Map 3; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, 'The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation', pp. 97–99; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Lothal Tentative List 5918, Description, consulted 17 November 2026; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Maritime Trade I. Pre-Islamic Period', section on Indus Valley and Persian Gulf connections, consulted 17 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: A reconstruction of Bronze Age maritime exchange in the Gulf region.

title: Maritime Routes to West Asia

body:
The names found in Mesopotamian texts

Mesopotamia was an ancient civilisation centred on the Tigris and Euphrates river region, principally in present-day Iraq. Its written records are valuable for understanding Harappan external trade because the Harappan script has not yet been deciphered.

Mesopotamian records dating to the third millennium BCE mention contacts with regions called Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha.

These names are important in understanding ancient trade, but they should not be treated as the names of 3 Harappan cities. They refer to geographical regions or trading partners mentioned in Mesopotamian sources.

Ancient nameProbable identificationTrade connection
DilmunBahrain and the surrounding Gulf regionAn important Persian Gulf trading centre.
MaganOman peninsulaParticularly associated with copper.
MeluhhaProbably the Harappan or Greater Indus regionAssociated with valuable goods and maritime contacts.

These identifications are widely used in historical scholarship, although the geographical extent of each ancient term is not always certain. In particular, the identification of Meluhha with the Harappan region is strongly supported but should not be presented as a decipherment of Harappan writing.

Commodities associated with Meluhha

Mesopotamian texts mention several valuable products associated with Meluhha:

  • Carnelian: a reddish semi-precious stone used for ornaments and beads.
  • Lapis lazuli: a valuable blue stone associated with sources in Afghanistan.
  • Copper: a metal used for tools, vessels and other manufactured articles.
  • Gold: a valuable metal used especially for ornaments.
  • Wood or timber: a useful material that also circulated through long-distance exchange networks.

The appearance of a product in a list of goods from Meluhha does not necessarily mean that the material was originally mined or produced within the central Harappan region. Some goods could have been obtained from neighbouring regions and exchanged again through Harappan networks.

Oman and the importance of copper

Copper provides an important example of the relationship between different trading regions.

Mesopotamian records associate Magan with copper. Archaeological evidence also suggests that copper from Oman probably reached the Harappan region.

The Harappans obtained copper from more than one possible source, including the Khetri region of Rajasthan and Oman. The existence of several sources means that copper moving through a trading network cannot automatically be assigned to one place of origin.

This distinction is useful when interpreting references to copper associated with Meluhha. A trading region could handle and redistribute goods that originated elsewhere.

Archaeological evidence supports the written references

Contacts with West Asia are supported by finds that can be compared with the Mesopotamian references.

  • Harappan-type seals and weights: examples have been discovered in the Persian Gulf region, showing connections with Harappan commercial practices.
  • Dilmun weights: weights associated with Dilmun followed the Harappan standard, an important indication of economic contact.
  • Persian Gulf-style seals: circular Gulf-type seals and Harappan motifs have been found in contexts linking the regions.
  • Carnelian beads: examples found at sites such as Susa in present-day Iran support the movement of valuable ornaments across long distances.
  • Harappan-type vessels in Oman: their presence provides further evidence of contact across the Arabian Sea.

Mesopotamian texts also refer to Meluhha as a land associated with seafarers. Together with depictions of boats and discoveries of objects in coastal regions, these references strengthen the conclusion that maritime exchange was an important part of Harappan external trade.

Written evidence and material evidence

Mesopotamian written records provide names of trading regions and references to commodities. Harappan objects discovered outside the Indus region provide physical evidence of contact. These forms of evidence support each other, but neither establishes the complete details of every commercial transaction.

What remains uncertain

The Harappan script remains undeciphered. Consequently, the precise names of individual merchants, the full rules of commercial exchange, the exact prices paid and the administrative arrangements governing trade cannot be reconstructed with certainty.

It is also important to distinguish an object of Harappan style from definite proof that its maker or owner belonged to the Harappan region. Styles and objects could circulate through contact, exchange and imitation.

The change after the Mature Harappan phase

After approximately 1900 BCE, many major Harappan cities declined or changed. Distinctive features such as standardised weights, seals, specialised urban crafts and extensive long-distance exchange became less prominent in many areas.

This change did not necessarily mean that all local exchange stopped. Settlements and economic activities continued in different forms, although the extensive urban trading system of the Mature Harappan period was no longer maintained in the same way.

Putting the trade system together

The main relationships can be understood as one connected system. Rural producers supplied food to towns. Materials such as carnelian, shell and copper reached specialised manufacturing centres. Goods moved through land, river and coastal routes. Standardised weights helped measure commodities, while seals and sealings could identify and protect consignments.

Gujarat contributed important centres such as Lothal, Dholavira and Nageshwar. External connections extended towards Oman, Bahrain and Mesopotamia, where the names Magan, Dilmun and Meluhha appear in written records.

Prelims focus

  • Dilmun: generally associated with Bahrain and the Persian Gulf region.
  • Magan: generally associated with Oman, especially its copper connections.
  • Meluhha: probably associated with the Harappan or Greater Indus region.
  • Mesopotamian texts mention carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper, gold and wood associated with Meluhha.
  • Dilmun weights followed the Harappan standard.
  • Trap: Mesopotamian records are readable sources of evidence; the Harappan script itself remains undeciphered.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones', Sections 6.2, 7 and 9, pp. 13–18; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, 'The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation', pp. 97–103; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Dholavira: a Harappan City', World Heritage List 1645, Brief Synthesis, consulted 17 November 2026; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Maritime Trade I. Pre-Islamic Period', discussion of Indus Valley and Persian Gulf trade, consulted 17 November 2026.]
